shots.script_line: For almost a century, nobody could fully explain the holes.
shots.visual: Extreme close-up of a wedge of Emmental cheese, slow push-in on the holes
shots.fallback: AI-generate a macro of a holed cheese wedge
shots.notes: Strong opening visual; the holes ARE the hook

shots.script_line: Everyone assumed it was just gas from bacteria.
shots.visual: Microscope / bubbling fermentation b-roll suggesting gas forming
shots.fallback: Motion graphic of CO2 bubbles rising

shots.script_line: But in 2015, Swiss scientists found the real trigger: tiny specks of hay.
shots.visual: Hay / dried grass in warm light, dust motes drifting; then a hand collecting fresh milk
shots.fallback: AI-generate hay dust drifting in a light beam

shots.script_line: Cleaner modern milking keeps the hay out — which is why the holes are shrinking.
shots.visual: Sterile modern stainless-steel milking equipment / dairy plant
shots.fallback: Motion graphic comparing holey vs hole-less cheese over time

shots.script_line: So the holes were never the bacteria's doing alone.
shots.visual: Final beauty shot: cheese wedge on a board, takeaway text on screen
shots.fallback: Stock cheese-on-board shot with text overlay
shots.notes: Carry the takeaway line; brand-accent color on the key word
